# typetag - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/typetag

## Expand description

**Serde serializable and deserializable trait objects.**

This crate provides a macro for painless serialization of `&dyn Trait` trait
objects and serialization + deserialization of `Box<dyn Trait>` trait
objects.

Let’s dive into the example and I’ll explain some more below.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Suppose I have a trait `WebEvent` and I require that every implementation of
the trait be serializable and deserializable so that I can send them to my
ad-serving AI. Here are just the types and trait impls to start with:

```
trait WebEvent {
    fn inspect(&self);
}
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct PageLoad;
impl WebEvent for PageLoad {
    fn inspect(&self) {
        println!("200 milliseconds or bust");
    }
}
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Click {
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
}
impl WebEvent for Click {
    fn inspect(&self) {
        println!("negative space between the ads: x={} y={}", self.x, self.y);
    }
}
```
We’ll need to be able to send an arbitrary web event as JSON to the AI:

```
fn send_event_to_money_factory(event: &dyn WebEvent) -> Result<()> {
    let json = serde_json::to_string(event)?;
    somehow_send_json(json)?;
    Ok(())
}
```
and receive an arbitrary web event as JSON on the server side:

```
fn process_event_from_clickfarm(json: &str) -> Result<()> {
    let event: Box<dyn WebEvent> = serde_json::from_str(json)?;
    overanalyze(event)?;
    Ok(())
}
```
The introduction claimed that this would be painless but I’ll let you be the judge.

First stick an attribute on top of the trait.

```
#[typetag::serde(tag = "type")]
trait WebEvent {
    fn inspect(&self);
}
```
Then stick a similar attribute on all those impl blocks too.

```
#[typetag::serde]
impl WebEvent for PageLoad {
    fn inspect(&self) {
        println!("200 milliseconds or bust");
    }
}
#[typetag::serde]
impl WebEvent for Click {
    fn inspect(&self) {
        println!("negative space between the ads: x={} y={}", self.x, self.y);
    }
}
```
And now it works as described. All in all, three lines were added!

[§](https://docs.rs#what)What?

Trait objects are serialized by this library like Serde enums. Every impl of the trait (anywhere in the program) looks like one variant of the enum.

All three of Serde’s tagged [enum representations](https://serde.rs/enum-representations.html) are supported. The one
shown above is the “internally tagged” style so our two event types would be
represented in JSON as:

```
{"type":"PageLoad"}
{"type":"Click","x":10,"y":10}
```
The choice of enum representation is controlled by the attribute that goes on the trait definition. Let’s check out the “adjacently tagged” style:

```
#[typetag::serde(tag = "type", content = "value")]
trait WebEvent {
    fn inspect(&self);
}
```
```
{"type":"PageLoad","value":null}
{"type":"Click","value":{"x":10,"y":10}}
```
and the “externally tagged” style, which is Serde’s default for enums:

```
#[typetag::serde]
trait WebEvent {
    fn inspect(&self);
}
```
```
{"PageLoad":null}
{"Click":{"x":10,"y":10}}
```
Separately, the value of the tag for a given trait impl may be defined as part of the attribute that goes on the trait impl. By default the tag will be the type name when no name is specified explicitly.

```
#[typetag::serde(name = "mouse_button_down")]
impl WebEvent for Click {
    fn inspect(&self) {
        println!("negative space between the ads: ({}, {})", self.x, self.y);
    }
}
```
`{"type":"mouse_button_down","x":10,"y":10}`Conceptually all you’re getting with this crate is that we build for you an enum in which every impl of the trait in your program is automatically registered as an enum variant. The behavior is the same as if you had written the enum yourself and implemented Serialize and Deserialize for the dyn Trait object in terms of the enum.

```
// generated (conceptually)
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
enum WebEvent {
    PageLoad(PageLoad),
    Click(Click),
    /* ... */
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#so-many-questions)So many questions

-
*Does it work if the trait impls are spread across different crates?***Yes**Serialization and deserialization both support every single impl of the trait across the dependency graph of the final program binary.
-
*Does it work in non-self-describing data formats like Bincode?***Yes**All three choices of enum representation will round-trip correctly through compact binary formats including Bincode.
-
*Does it support non-struct types?***Yes**The implementations of the trait can be structs, enums, primitives, or anything else supported by Serde. The Serialize and Deserialize impls may be derived or handwritten.
-
*Even in WebAssembly?***Yes**Wasm is supported but with some extra setup described [here](https://docs.rs/inventory/0.3/inventory/index.html#webassembly-and-constructors).
-
*Didn’t someone explain to me why this wasn’t possible?***Yes**It might have been me.
-
*Then how does it work?*We use the `inventory``ctor``Box<dyn Trait>`deserialization will perform the work of iterating the registry and building a map of tags to deserialization functions. Subsequent deserializations find the right deserialization function in that map. The`erased-serde`

# inventory - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/inventory/0.3/inventory/index.html

## Expand description

**Typed distributed plugin registration.**

This crate provides a way to set up a plugin registry into which plugins can be registered from any source file linked into your application. There does not need to be a central list of all the plugins.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Suppose we are writing a command line flags library and want to allow any source file in the application to register command line flags that are relevant to it.

This is the flag registration style used by [gflags](https://gflags.github.io/gflags/) and is better suited
for large scale development than maintaining a single central list of flags,
as the central list would become an endless source of merge conflicts in an
application developed simultaneously by thousands of developers.

[§](https://docs.rs#instantiating-the-plugin-registry)Instantiating the plugin registry

Let’s use a `struct Flag` as the plugin type, which will contain the short
name of the flag like `-v`, the full name like `--verbose`, and maybe other
information like argument type and help text. We instantiate a plugin
registry with an invocation of `inventory::collect!`.

```
pub struct Flag {
    short: char,
    name: &'static str,
    /* ... */
}
impl Flag {
    pub const fn new(short: char, name: &'static str) -> Self {
        Flag { short, name }
    }
}
inventory::collect!(Flag);
```
This `collect!` call must be in the same crate that defines the plugin type.
This macro does not “run” anything so place it outside of any function body.

[§](https://docs.rs#registering-plugins)Registering plugins

Now any crate with access to the `Flag` type can register flags as a plugin.
Plugins can be registered by the same crate that declares the plugin type,
or by any downstream crate.

```
inventory::submit! {
    Flag::new('v', "verbose")
}
```
The `submit!` macro does not “run” anything so place it outside of any
function body. In particular, note that all `submit!` invocations across all
source files linked into your application all take effect simultaneously. A
`submit!` invocation is not a statement that needs to be called from `main`
in order to execute.

[§](https://docs.rs#iterating-over-plugins)Iterating over plugins

The value `inventory::iter::<T>` is an iterator with element type `&'static T` that iterates over all plugins registered of type `T`.

```
for flag in inventory::iter::<Flag> {
    println!("-{}, --{}", flag.short, flag.name);
}
```
There is no guarantee about the order that plugins of the same type are visited by the iterator. They may be visited in any order.

[§](https://docs.rs#webassembly-and-constructors)WebAssembly and constructors

`inventory` supports all WebAssembly targets, including
`wasm*-unknown-unknown`. However, in unusual circumstances, ensuring that
constructors run may require some extra effort. The Wasm linker will
synthesize a function `extern "C" unsafe fn __wasm_call_ctors()` which calls
all constructors when invoked; this function will *not* be exported from the
module unless you do so explicitly. Depending on the result of a heuristic,
the linker may or may not insert a call to this function from the beginning
of every function that your module exports. Specifically, it regards a
module as having “command-style linkage” if:

- it is not relocatable;
- it is not a position-independent executable;
- and it does not call `__wasm_call_ctors`, directly or indirectly, from any exported function.

The linker expects that the embedder will call into a command-style module
only once per instantiation. Violation of this expectation can result in
`__wasm_call_ctors` being called multiple times. This is dangerous in
general, but safe and mostly harmless in the case of constructors generated
by `inventory`, which are idempotent.

If you are building a module which relies on constructors and may be called
into multiple times per instance, you should export `__wasm_call_ctors` (or
a wrapper around it) and ensure that the embedder calls it immediately after
instantiation. Even though `inventory` may work fine without this, it is
still good practice, because it avoids unnecessary overhead from repeated
constructor invocation. It also can prevent unsoundness if some of your
constructors are generated by other crates or other programming languages.

```
#[cfg(target_family = "wasm")]
unsafe extern "C" {
    fn __wasm_call_ctors();
}
fn main() {
    #[cfg(target_family = "wasm")]
    unsafe {
        __wasm_call_ctors();
    }
}
```
## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [submit](https://docs.rs/macro.submit.html)
- Enter an element into the plugin registry corresponding to its type.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Collect](https://docs.rs/trait.Collect.html)

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

# star_toml - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/star-toml/26.7.2/star_toml/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#star_toml--load-layer-and-validate-any-toml-config-file)star_toml — load, layer, and validate any `*.toml` config file

`star_toml` (pronounced “star TOML”, as in `*.toml`) is a self-contained
Rust framework for any TOML configuration file. Three concerns, one crate:

- **Loading**— parse a single file, compose multiple sources in layers, expand- `${ENV_VARS}`, walk parent dirs to discover config files.
- **Validation**— Pydantic-style engine that collects- *every*error at once, each with a path-precise location, the offending value, and a machine-matchable code.
- **Analytics**— Van der Aalst-grade extensions: conformance fitness, variant fingerprinting, DECLARE cross-field constraints, severity stratification.

Dependencies: `serde`, `toml`, `thiserror`. No async, no proc-macros, no allocator
tricks, no crypto.

[§](https://docs.rs#decision-guide--which-api-for-which-task)Decision guide — which API for which task?

| Task | Use |
|---|---|
| Parse a TOML string | `from_str::<T>(s)` |
| Load one file | `load_file::<T>(path)` |
| Walk parent dirs to find a file | /`find_config_file``find_and_load` |
| Merge defaults + file + env | builder`Loader` |
| Remember where the file is (relative paths) | →`Loader::load_file``ConfigFile<T>` |
| Parse + validate in one call | `Loader::load_validated` |
| Serialize back to TOML | /`to_string``save_file` |
| Recursive table merge | `deep_merge` |
| `${VAR}`substitution alone | `expand_env_vars` |
| Validate an already-loaded struct | /`Validate::check``Validate::validated` |
| Validate without a Rust struct | declarative builder`Schema` |
| Attach severity / cross-field rules | /`Validator::with_severity``Validator::check_consistent` |
| Get conformance score | `ValidationErrors::fitness` |
| Fingerprint error pattern | `ValidationErrors::variant_id` |

[§](https://docs.rs#complete-public-api)Complete public API

[§](https://docs.rs#loading)Loading

| Symbol | Kind | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `from_str` | fn | Expand env vars, parse TOML, deserialize to `T` |
| `load_file` | fn | Read, expand, parse a `.toml`file |
| `find_config_file` | fn | Walk parent dirs for `name`; returns`Option<PathBuf>` |
| `find_and_load` | fn | +`find_config_file`combined`load_file` |
| `Loader` | struct | Builder: chain `.layer_str`,`.find_file`,`.env_prefix`, then`.load()` |
| `ConfigFile<T>` | struct | Loaded config + path; `.resolve(rel)`anchors relative paths |
| `to_string` | fn | Serialize `T: Serialize`to a TOML string |
| `save_file` | fn | Serialize to disk, creating parent dirs as needed |
| `deep_merge` | fn | Recursively merge two `toml::Value`s (later wins) |
| `expand_env_vars` | fn | `${VAR}`/`$VAR`substitution; unknown vars left intact |

[§](https://docs.rs#validation-pydantic--van-der-aalst)Validation (Pydantic + Van der Aalst)

| Symbol | Kind | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `Schema` | struct | Declarative builder: validate `toml::Value`/ TOML strings without a Rust struct |
| `FieldBuilder` | struct | Fluent constraint chain returned by `Schema::field` |
| `Validate` | trait | Implement `validate(&self, v: &mut Validator)`on your config type |
| `Validator` | struct | Accumulates errors; carries the current path location |
| `Validator::field` | method | Descend into table key `name`for the duration of a closure |
| `Validator::index` | method | Descend into array index `i`for the duration of a closure |
| `Validator::with_severity` | method | Set for all checks inside a closure`Severity` |
| `Validator::check_non_empty` | method | Fail if `&str`is empty → code`empty` |
| `Validator::check_range` | method | Fail if value outside `lo..=hi`→ code`out_of_range` |
| `Validator::check_one_of` | method | Fail if value not in allowed set → code `not_one_of` |
| `Validator::check_predicate` | method | Custom boolean check with caller-defined code |
| `Validator::check_consistent` | method | DECLARE cross-field constraint → code `Inconsistent` |
| `Validator::error` | method | Record a raw at the current location`ErrorKind` |
| `Validator::error_with` | method | Same, capturing the offending value as a string |
| `Validator::finish` | method | Consume validator → `Ok(())`or`Err(ValidationErrors)` |
| `ValidationErrors` | struct | Non-empty collection of failures; implements `Display`+`Error` |
| `ValidationErrors::errors` | method | Slice of individual s`ValidationError` |
| `ValidationErrors::len` | method | Error count |
| `ValidationErrors::fitness` | method | Conformance score: `checks_passed / checks_run`(0.0–1.0) |
| `ValidationErrors::variant_id` | method | FNV-1a fingerprint of the error pattern |
| `ValidationErrors::by_section` | method | Group errors by top-level config section |
| `ValidationErrors::has_fatal` | method | True if any error is `Severity::Fatal` |
| `ValidationErrors::errors_above` | method | Filter to errors at or above a severity level |
| `ValidationError` | struct | One failure: `loc`,`kind`,`severity`,`input`,`msg` |
| `ValidationError::code` | method | Stable string code ( `"empty"`,`"out_of_range"`, …) |
| `ValidationError::repair_hint` | method | Auto-derived minimum fix for this error kind |
| `ValidationError::is_fatal` | method | True when `severity == Severity::Fatal` |
| `ErrorKind` | enum | Structured reason: `Empty`,`OutOfRange`,`NotOneOf`,`Inconsistent`, … |
| `Loc` | struct | Path into the config tree, e.g. `server.tls.port`or`[2].name` |
| `LocSegment` | enum | `Key(String)`or`Index(usize)` |
| `Severity` | enum | `Advisory`<`Warning`<`Error`<`Fatal` |

[§](https://docs.rs#error-types)Error types

| Variant | When |
|---|---|
| `Error::FileNotFound` | File does not exist |
| `Error::Io` | OS error reading / writing a file |
| `Error::Parse` | TOML syntax or serde deserialization error |
| `Error::Serialize` | `toml::to_string`failed |
| `Error::Invalid` | Wraps ; returned by`ValidationErrors``Loader::load_validated` |
| `Error::Validation` | Lower-level validation string; rarely produced by this crate |

[§](https://docs.rs#patterns-cookbook-copy-pasteable)Patterns cookbook (copy-pasteable)

[§](https://docs.rs#pattern-1--load-a-single-file)Pattern 1 — load a single file

```
use star_toml::load_file;
#[derive(serde::Deserialize)]
struct AppConfig { name: String, port: u16 }
let cfg: AppConfig = load_file("app.toml")?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#pattern-2--layered-loading-defaults--file--env)Pattern 2 — layered loading (defaults + file + env)

```
use star_toml::Loader;
#[derive(serde::Deserialize)]
struct Cfg { name: String, port: u16 }
const DEFAULTS: &str = "name = 'my-app'\nport = 8080\n";
let cfg: Cfg = Loader::new()
    .layer_str(DEFAULTS, "built-in defaults")  // lowest priority
    .find_file("app.toml")                      // walk up from cwd
    .layer_file_if_exists("~/.config/app.toml") // optional user overrides
    .env_prefix("APP_")                         // APP_PORT=9090 → port = 9090
    .load()?;                                   // highest priority
```
[§](https://docs.rs#pattern-3--load--validate-in-one-call)Pattern 3 — load + validate in one call

```
use star_toml::{Loader, Validate, Validator};
#[derive(serde::Deserialize)]
struct Cfg { port: u16 }
impl Validate for Cfg {
    fn validate(&self, v: &mut Validator) {
        v.check_range("port", self.port, 1024..=65535);
    }
}
// Fails with Error::Invalid(ValidationErrors) if any rule is violated.
let cfg: Cfg = Loader::new().find_file("server.toml").load_validated()?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#pattern-4--collect-all-errors-render-pydantic-style)Pattern 4 — collect all errors, render Pydantic-style

```
use star_toml::{Validate, Validator};
struct Server { host: String, port: u16 }
struct App { name: String, workers: u32, server: Server }
impl Validate for Server {
    fn validate(&self, v: &mut Validator) {
        v.check_non_empty("host", &self.host);
        v.check_range("port", self.port, 1..=65535);
    }
}
impl Validate for App {
    fn validate(&self, v: &mut Validator) {
        v.check_non_empty("name", &self.name);
        v.check_range("workers", self.workers, 1..=1024);
        v.field("server", |v| self.server.validate(v)); // nested → server.*
    }
}
let app = App {
    name: String::new(),
    workers: 0,
    server: Server { host: String::new(), port: 0 },
};
let report = app.check().unwrap_err();
assert_eq!(report.len(), 4); // ALL four errors, not just the first
let locs: Vec<String> = report.errors().iter().map(|e| e.loc.to_string()).collect();
assert_eq!(locs, ["name", "workers", "server.host", "server.port"]);
// Renders as:
// 4 validation errors for App
// name
//   must not be empty (got: `""`) [empty]
// ...
println!("{report}");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#pattern-5--severity-levels--repair-hints)Pattern 5 — severity levels + repair hints

```
use star_toml::{Validate, Validator, Severity};
struct Cfg { log_dir: String, port: u16 }
impl Validate for Cfg {
    fn validate(&self, v: &mut Validator) {
        // Hard error: port is required
        v.check_range("port", self.port, 1024..=65535);
        // Advisory: non-critical best-practice hint
        v.with_severity(Severity::Advisory, |v| {
            v.check_non_empty("log_dir", &self.log_dir);
        });
    }
}
let errs = Cfg { port: 0, log_dir: String::new() }.check().unwrap_err();
assert!(!errs.has_fatal());
for e in errs.errors() {
    println!("[{}] {} → fix: {}", e.severity, e.loc, e.repair_hint());
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#pattern-6--van-der-aalst-analytics)Pattern 6 — Van der Aalst analytics

```
use star_toml::{Validate, Validator};
struct Pair { a: u32, b: u32 }
impl Validate for Pair {
    fn validate(&self, v: &mut Validator) {
        v.check_range("a", self.a, 1..=10); // passes
        v.check_range("b", self.b, 1..=10); // fails
    }
}
let errs = Pair { a: 5, b: 0 }.check().unwrap_err();
// Conformance fitness: how much of the model the config satisfies
assert_eq!(errs.fitness(), 0.5); // 1 of 2 checks passed
// Variant fingerprint: same error pattern = same ID across runs
let id = errs.variant_id();
assert_eq!(Pair { a: 9, b: 0 }.check().unwrap_err().variant_id(), id);
// Object-centric grouping: errors by top-level config section
for (section, errors) in errs.by_section() {
    println!("{section}: {} error(s)", errors.len());
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#pattern-7--declare-cross-field-constraint)Pattern 7 — DECLARE cross-field constraint

```
use star_toml::{Validate, Validator};
struct Tls { enabled: bool, cert_path: String }
impl Validate for Tls {
    fn validate(&self, v: &mut Validator) {
        // Co-existence: TLS enabled ⟺ cert_path non-empty
        v.check_consistent(
            "cert_path",            // primary field (where error is recorded)
            &["enabled"],           // related fields (tagged in ErrorKind::Inconsistent)
            !self.enabled || !self.cert_path.is_empty(),
            "tls_cert_required",    // stable machine-matchable code
            "cert_path must be set when TLS is enabled",
        );
    }
}
let bad = Tls { enabled: true, cert_path: String::new() };
let errs = bad.check().unwrap_err();
assert_eq!(errs.errors()[0].code(), "tls_cert_required");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#pattern-8--validate-arrays-element-by-element)Pattern 8 — validate arrays element-by-element

```
use star_toml::{Validate, Validator};
struct Pipeline(Vec<String>);
impl Validate for Pipeline {
    fn validate(&self, v: &mut Validator) {
        for (i, stage) in self.0.iter().enumerate() {
            v.index(i, |v| v.check_non_empty("name", stage));
        }
    }
}
let p = Pipeline(vec!["build".into(), String::new(), "test".into()]);
let errs = p.check().unwrap_err();
assert_eq!(errs.errors()[0].loc.to_string(), "[1].name");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#pattern-9--source-relative-path-resolution)Pattern 9 — source-relative path resolution

```
use star_toml::{Loader, ConfigFile};
#[derive(serde::Deserialize)]
struct Build { template_dir: String }
let cf: ConfigFile<Build> = Loader::new().find_file("build.toml").load_file()?;
// Resolved relative to the directory that contains build.toml,
// not relative to the current working directory.
let abs = cf.resolve(&cf.config.template_dir);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#pattern-10--write-back)Pattern 10 — write-back

```
use star_toml::save_file;
#[derive(serde::Serialize)]
struct Config { name: String, port: u16 }
save_file(&Config { name: "app".into(), port: 8080 }, "ggen.toml")?;
// Parent directories are created automatically.
```
[§](https://docs.rs#layer-merge-semantics)Layer merge semantics

Layers merge left-to-right (later = higher priority).

- **Tables**: keys merged recursively — a later layer overrides one key without erasing siblings.
- **Arrays, scalars**: later layer replaces earlier entirely.

```
use toml::Value;
use star_toml::deep_merge;
let mut base: Value = toml::from_str("[db]\nhost=\"localhost\"\nport=5432\n").unwrap();
let overlay: Value = toml::from_str("[db]\nport=5433\n").unwrap();
deep_merge(&mut base, overlay);
// host preserved, port overridden
assert_eq!(base["db"]["host"].as_str(), Some("localhost"));
assert_eq!(base["db"]["port"].as_integer(), Some(5433));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#environment-variable-mapping)Environment variable mapping

`.env_prefix("APP_")` maps env vars to TOML keys:

- Prefix stripped: `APP_PORT`→`port`
- Double underscore as dot: `APP_SERVER__PORT`→`server.port`
- Value coercion: `"true"`→ bool,`"42"`→ integer,`"3.14"`→ float, otherwise string

Inline `${VAR}` / `$VAR` patterns in TOML sources are expanded before parsing.
Unknown variables are left as-is (safe for partial expansion).

```
use star_toml::expand_env_vars;
std::env::set_var("MY_HOST", "prod.example.com");
let out = expand_env_vars("host = \"${MY_HOST}\"");
assert_eq!(out, "host = \"prod.example.com\"");
std::env::remove_var("MY_HOST");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#error-handling)Error handling

All fallible free functions return [ Result<T>](https://docs.rs/error/type.Result.html) =

`Result<T, Error>`.
The most common error is [from](https://docs.rs/error/enum.Error.html#variant.Invalid)

`Error::Invalid`[; downcast with](https://docs.rs/loader/struct.Loader.html#method.load_validated)

`Loader::load_validated``if let Error::Invalid(report) = err { … }`.```
use star_toml::{Loader, Validate, Validator, Error};
#[derive(serde::Deserialize)]
struct Cfg { port: u16 }
impl Validate for Cfg {
    fn validate(&self, v: &mut Validator) {
        v.check_range("port", self.port, 1024..=65535);
    }
}
match Loader::new().find_file("server.toml").load_validated::<Cfg>() {
    Ok(cfg) => println!("port = {}", cfg.port),
    Err(Error::FileNotFound(p)) => eprintln!("config not found: {}", p.display()),
    Err(Error::Parse { source, .. }) => eprintln!("TOML syntax: {source}"),
    Err(Error::Invalid(report)) => {
        eprintln!("{report}");
        for e in report.errors() {
            eprintln!("  fix {} → {}", e.loc, e.repair_hint());
        }
    }
    Err(e) => eprintln!("other error: {e}"),
}
```

# zebra_state - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/zebra-state/10.0.0/zebra_state/

## Expand description

State contextual verification and storage code for Zebra.

[§](https://docs.rs#correctness)Correctness

Await UTXO and block commit requests should be wrapped in a timeout, because:

- await UTXO requests wait for a block containing that UTXO, and
- contextual verification and state updates wait for all previous blocks.

Otherwise, verification of out-of-order and invalid blocks can hang indefinitely.

# smos - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/smos/0.3.5/smos/

## Expand description

`smos` — concrete implementations of the application-layer ports.

This crate is the *only* place IO happens in the SMOS Rust port. Each
adapter implements a `smos_application::ports` trait against a specific
external system (SurrealDB for persistence, system clock for time, HTTP
for LLM upstream, OpenAI-compatible `llama-server` endpoints for
embeddings/extraction/rerank, ort + ONNX Runtime for NLI).

See `smos-poc/ТРЕБОВАНИЯ.md` for the canonical specification and
`smos-application` for the port shapes.

# rsclaw_embed - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rsclaw-embed/0.1.0/rsclaw_embed/

## Expand description

Shared text-embedding stack — used by both the agent memory
subsystem (`src/agent/memory.rs`) and the knowledge base
(`src/kb/`). Extracted from `agent/memory.rs` so the two don’t
each ship their own embedder.

Backends (all behind the `Embedder` trait, hot-swappable):

- `FnvEmbedder`— deterministic hash projection, no model.
- `LocalBgeEmbedder`— candle BGE (BERT) from a model dir.
- `OpenAiEmbedder`— OpenAI-compatible- `/v1/embeddings`REST; point- `base_url`at a GPU fleet running Qwen3-Embedding for remote acceleration.
- `OllamaEmbedder`— Ollama local REST API.

`agent::memory` re-exports these names for backward compatibility,
so existing `EmbedderBackend (agent crate)` paths keep
working.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use fleet::`- [FleetHttp](https://docs.rs/fleet/struct.FleetHttp.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [fleet](https://docs.rs/fleet/index.html)
- Shared rsclaw fleet HTTP client with 307/308 redirect caching.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_EMBED_DIM.html)- EMBED_ - DIM
- Fallback embedding dimension when no model is loaded (FNV).
- [OLLAMA_](https://docs.rs/constant.OLLAMA_DEFAULT_MODEL.html)- DEFAULT_ - MODEL
- Default Ollama embedding model.
- [OLLAMA_](https://docs.rs/constant.OLLAMA_DEFAULT_URL.html)- DEFAULT_ - URL
- Default Ollama REST base URL.
- [OPENAI_](https://docs.rs/constant.OPENAI_DEFAULT_BASE_URL.html)- DEFAULT_ - BASE_ - URL
- Default OpenAI-compatible API root. Override to point at a GPU fleet
serving `/v1/embeddings`(vLLM / SGLang / TEI / infinity).
- [OPENAI_](https://docs.rs/constant.OPENAI_DEFAULT_MODEL.html)- DEFAULT_ - MODEL
- Default OpenAI-compatible embedding model name.
- [QWEN3_](https://docs.rs/constant.QWEN3_DEFAULT_QUERY_INSTRUCTION.html)- DEFAULT_ - QUERY_ - INSTRUCTION
- Default query-side instruction for instruction-aware embedding models. Wording follows the Qwen3-Embedding model card’s retrieval default.
- [RSCLAW_](https://docs.rs/constant.RSCLAW_API_BASE_URL.html)- API_ - BASE_ - URL
- RsClaw fleet’s OpenAI/Cohere-compatible API root (embeddings, rerank,
ocr). Convention-over-config: a `rsclaw-*`model name with no explicit base_url resolves here, mirroring the rsclaw chat provider’s treatment.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Embedder](https://docs.rs/trait.Embedder.html)
- Pluggable text → vector backend. Implementors are interchangeable at
runtime — see `MemoryStore::begin_swap`for the hot-migration path used to upgrade from FNV → BGE (or BGE-small → BGE-base) without restart.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [build_](https://docs.rs/fn.build_remote_client.html)- remote_ - client
- Shared HTTP client for remote embedding/rerank endpoints.
- [format_](https://docs.rs/fn.format_query.html)- query
- Build the text to embed for a retrieval *query*. With no instruction (or an empty one) the query is embedded as-is, preserving symmetric behaviour. When an instruction is set, wrap it in the Qwen3-Embedding query format (`Instruct: {task}\nQuery: {query}`), which materially improves asymmetric retrieval quality. Document embeddings never use this.
- [is_](https://docs.rs/fn.is_rsclaw_model.html)- rsclaw_ - model
- True for first-party fleet model names (`rsclaw-embedding-v1`,`rsclaw-reranker-v1`,`rsclaw-ocr-v1`, …).
- [openai_](https://docs.rs/fn.openai_model_dim.html)- model_ - dim
- Best-effort output dimension for a known OpenAI-compatible model name.
Callers should prefer an explicit `memorySearch.dimensions`when the model isn’t in this table.
- [resolve_](https://docs.rs/fn.resolve_embed_base_url.html)- embed_ - base_ - url
- Resolve the effective API root: an explicit `base_url`always wins; otherwise a`rsclaw-*`model defaults to the fleet, and anything else to OpenAI. Empty/whitespace base_url counts as unset.
- [resolve_](https://docs.rs/fn.resolve_query_instruction.html)- query_ - instruction
- Resolve the effective query instruction for an embed config: an explicit
`queryInstruction`always wins; otherwise instruction-aware models (Qwen3-Embedding) get`QWEN3_DEFAULT_QUERY_INSTRUCTION`

# zebra_network - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/zebra-network/10.0.0/zebra_network/

## Expand description

Networking code for Zebra.

[§](https://docs.rs#network-protocol-design)Network Protocol Design

The Zcash network protocol is inherited from Bitcoin, which uses a stateful network protocol in which messages can arrive in any order (even before a handshake is complete!). The same Bitcoin message may be a request or a response depending on context.

[§](https://docs.rs#achieving-concurrency)Achieving Concurrency

This crate translates the legacy Zcash network protocol
into a stateless, request-response oriented protocol defined by
the [ Request](https://docs.rs/enum.Request.html) and

[enums.](https://docs.rs/enum.Response.html)

`Response``zebra-network` completely
encapsulates all peer handling code behind a single
[representing “the network”, which load-balances outbound](https://docs.rs/tower-service/0.3.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tower_service/trait.Service.html)

`tower::Service`[s over available peers.](https://docs.rs/enum.Request.html)

`Request`Unlike the underlying legacy network protocol, Zebra’s `PeerSet`
[ tower::Service](https://docs.rs/tower-service/0.3.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tower_service/trait.Service.html) guarantees that each

`Request` future will resolve to the
correct `Response`, rather than an unrelated `Response` message.Each peer connection is handled by a distinct [`peer::Connection`] task.
The Zcash network protocol is bidirectional, so Zebra interprets incoming
Zcash messages as either:

- `Response`- `Request`
- inbound `Request``tower::Service`

All connection state is isolated to individual peers, so this
design is structurally immune to the recent `ping` attack.

[§](https://docs.rs#connection-pool)Connection Pool

Because [ tower::Service](https://docs.rs/tower-service/0.3.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tower_service/trait.Service.html)s provide backpressure information, we
can dynamically manage the size of the connection pool according
to inbound and outbound demand.  The inbound service can shed load
when it is not ready for requests, causing those peer connections
to close, and the outbound service can connect to additional peers
when it is overloaded.

[§](https://docs.rs#zebra-network-structure)`zebra-network` Structure

[ init](https://docs.rs/fn.init.html) is the main entry point for

`zebra-network`.
It uses the following services, tasks, and endpoints:[§](https://docs.rs#low-level-network-connections)Low-Level Network Connections

Inbound Zcash Listener Task:

- accepts inbound connections on the listener port
- initiates Zcash [`peer::Handshake`]s, which creates [`peer::Connection`] tasks for each inbound connection

Outbound Zcash Connector Service:

- initiates outbound connections to peer addresses
- initiates Zcash [`peer::Handshake`]s, which creates [`peer::Connection`] tasks for each outbound connection

Zebra uses direct TCP connections to share blocks and mempool transactions with other peers.

The [`isolated`] APIs provide anonymised TCP and [Tor](https://crates.io/crates/arti)
connections to individual peers.
These isolated connections can be used to send user-generated transactions anonymously.
Tor connections are currently disabled until `arti-client`’s dependency `x25519-dalek v1.2.0`
is updated to a higher version. See #5492.

[§](https://docs.rs#individual-peer-connections)Individual Peer Connections

Each new peer connection spawns the following tasks:

[ peer::Client](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html) Service:

- provides an interface for outbound requests to an individual peer

[`peer::Connection`] Service:

- manages connection state: awaiting a request, or handling an inbound or outbound response
- provides an interface for inbound requests from an individual peer
- drops peer connections if the inbound request queue is overloaded

Since the Zcash network protocol is bidirectional, inbound and outbound connections are handled using the same logic.

[§](https://docs.rs#connection-pool-1)Connection Pool

`PeerSet` Network Service:

- provides an interface for other services and tasks running within this node
to make requests to remote peers (“the rest of the network”)
- accepts `Request`
- sends each request to a `peer::Client`
- returns the `Response``peer::Client`

- accepts

Inbound Network Service:

- provides an interface for remote peers to request data held by this node

Note: the inbound service is implemented by the [ init](https://docs.rs/fn.init.html) caller.

Peer Inventory Service:

- tracks gossiped `inv`advertisements for each peer
- updated before each `PeerSet`request is processed
- tracks missing inventory for each peer
- used by the `PeerSet`to route block and transaction requests to peers that have the requested data

[§](https://docs.rs#peer-discovery)Peer Discovery

[ AddressBook](https://docs.rs/struct.AddressBook.html) Service:

- maintains a list of peer addresses and associated connection attempt metadata
- address book metadata is used to prioritise peer connection attempts
- updated by an independent thread based on peer connection status changes
- caches peer addresses to disk regularly using an independent task

Initial Seed Peer Task: On startup:

- loads seed peers from the config, resolving them via DNS if required
- loads cached peer addresses from disk
- initiates new outbound peer connections to seed and cached peers
- adds seed and cached peer addresses to the `AddressBook`

Peer Crawler Task:

- discovers new peer addresses by sending `Addr`requests to connected peers
- initiates new outbound peer connections in response to application demand

# num_bigint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-bigint/0.5.0/num_bigint/

## Expand description

Big Integer Types for Rust

- A `BigUint`
- A `BigInt``BigUint``Sign`

Common numerical operations are overloaded, so we can treat them the same way we treat other numbers.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use num_bigint::BigUint;
use num_traits::One;
// Calculate large fibonacci numbers.
fn fib(n: usize) -> BigUint {
    let mut f0 = BigUint::ZERO;
    let mut f1 = BigUint::ONE;
    for _ in 0..n {
        let f2 = f0 + &f1;
        f0 = f1;
        f1 = f2;
    }
    f0
}
// This is a very large number.
println!("fib(1000) = {}", fib(1000));
```
It’s easy to generate large random numbers:

```
use rand::{SeedableRng, rngs::SmallRng};
use num_bigint::{BigInt, BigRng010};
// This seed is just for demonstration, but in most cases
// you'll probably want a non-deterministic `rng`.
let mut rng = SmallRng::seed_from_u64(42);
let a = rng.random_bigint(1000);
let low = BigInt::from(-10000);
let high = BigInt::from(10000);
let b = rng.random_bigint_range(&low, &high);
// Probably an even larger number.
println!("{}", a * b);
```
See the “Features” section for instructions for enabling random number generation.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

The `std` crate feature is enabled by default, which enables [ std::error::Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/error/trait.Error.html)
implementations and some internal use of floating point approximations. This can be disabled by
depending on

`num-bigint` with `default-features = false`. Either way, the `alloc` crate is
always required for heap allocation of the [/](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)

`BigInt`[digits.](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)

`BigUint`[§](https://docs.rs#random-generation)Random Generation

`num-bigint` supports the generation of random big integers when either of the `rand_0_9` or
`rand_0_10` features are enabled. The [ BigRng09](https://docs.rs/trait.BigRng09.html) and

[traits provide extension methods for any](https://docs.rs/trait.BigRng010.html)

`BigRng010``rand_core` RNG of their respective version, while the structs [,](https://docs.rs/struct.RandomBits.html)

`RandomBits`[, and](https://docs.rs/struct.UniformBigInt.html)

`UniformBigInt`[fulfill further functionality for random distributions in](https://docs.rs/struct.UniformBigUint.html)

`UniformBigUint``rand::distr`.For example, using `rand v0.10` in your `Cargo.toml` may look like this:

```
rand = "0.10"
num-bigint = { version = "0.5", features = ["rand_0_10"] }
```
Note that you must use the same version of `rand` as the feature you enable in `num-bigint`.
It’s also fine for multiple versions to be enabled at once – the random-distribution structs
will be shared with trait implementations for each `rand` feature that is enabled, while the
`BigRng` traits are distinct.

You can instead use `rand_core_0_9` or `rand_core_0_10` for a more restricted subset, with
*only* the `BigRng` traits.

[§](https://docs.rs#arbitrary-big-integers)Arbitrary Big Integers

`num-bigint` supports `arbitrary` and `quickcheck` features to implement
[ arbitrary::Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/arbitrary/1.1.6/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arbitrary/trait.Arbitrary.html) and

[, respectively, for both](https://docs.rs/quickcheck/1.0.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/quickcheck/arbitrary/trait.Arbitrary.html)

`quickcheck::Arbitrary`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)

`BigInt`[. These are useful for fuzzing and other forms of randomized testing.](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)

`BigUint`[§](https://docs.rs#serialization)Serialization

The `serde` feature adds implementations of [ Serialize](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/trait.Serialize.html) and

[for both](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/de/trait.Deserialize.html)

`Deserialize`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)

`BigInt`[. Their serialized data is generated portably, regardless of platform differences like the internal digit size.](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)

`BigUint`[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility)Compatibility

The `num-bigint` crate is tested for rustc 1.60 and greater.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [BigInt](https://docs.rs/struct.BigInt.html)
- A big signed integer type.
- [BigUint](https://docs.rs/struct.BigUint.html)

# noesis_bevy - Rust

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [animation](https://docs.rs/animation/index.html)
- Per-view code-built property animations: the runtime-driven counterpart to a
XAML `<Storyboard>`/`<DoubleAnimation>`declared inline in a`ControlTemplate`or`Style.Triggers`.
- [bake](https://docs.rs/bake/index.html)
- Bake an XAML view to an offscreen `Handle<Image>`
- [binding](https://docs.rs/binding/index.html)
- Per-view value-converter / multi-binding bridge: install a code-built
`{Binding}`, driven by a**Rust**`ValueConverter``MultiValueConverter`
- [brushes](https://docs.rs/brushes/index.html)
- Per-view code-built brush bridge: paint named XAML elements with brushes
constructed in Rust, no XAML authoring required. The brush counterpart of the
`crate::dp``crate::geometry`
- [classes](https://docs.rs/classes/index.html)
- Register Rust-backed XAML classes (`<myns:Foo>`) with Noesis from Bevy systems.
- [commands](https://docs.rs/commands/index.html)
- Per-view Rust-owned `ICommand`bridge.
- [diagnostics](https://docs.rs/diagnostics/index.html)
- App-level diagnostics bridge: surface Noesis’s process-global allocator counters as a Bevy resource and route its error handler into Bevy’s log.
- [dp](https://docs.rs/dp/index.html)
- Per-view generic dependency-property get/set bridge, keyed by
`(x:Name, property)`.
- [events](https://docs.rs/events/index.html)
- Per-view routed-event bridge: surface `BaseButton::Click`and`UIElement::KeyDown`from named elements of a single`crate::NoesisView`**and**Bevy`EntityEvent`s (observers).
- [focus](https://docs.rs/focus/index.html)
- Per-view keyboard-focus bridge: give a named XAML element keyboard
focus on a single `crate::NoesisView`
- [focus_](https://docs.rs/focus_input/index.html)- input
- Per-view focus-navigation and input-binding bridge: the directional,
engagement, and key-chord layer on top of the one-shot `crate::NoesisFocus`
- [font](https://docs.rs/font/index.html)
- Font-asset plumbing for the Bevy plugin.
- [geometry](https://docs.rs/geometry/index.html)
- Per-view geometry bridge: imperative vector polyline writes against named
XAML `Path`elements on a single`NoesisView``crate::text`
- [headless](https://docs.rs/headless/index.html)
- Headless harness entry point for tests and CI.
- [image](https://docs.rs/image/index.html)
- Image-asset plumbing for the `ImageBrush`/`Image`loader.
- [imaging](https://docs.rs/imaging/index.html)
- Per-view code-built imaging bridge: drive a named `<Image>`’s pixels from a Rust-provided bitmap (RGBA8 + size), no image file on disk required. The imaging counterpart of the`crate::brushes``crate::geometry`
- [inlines](https://docs.rs/inlines/index.html)
- Per-view **formatted text**bridge: give a named`TextBlock`rich inline content (`Run`/`Bold`/`Italic`/`Underline`/`Span`/`Hyperlink`/`LineBreak`) from Bevy, then read the resulting live structure back.
- [input](https://docs.rs/input/index.html)
- Bevy → Noesis input forwarding.
- [integration](https://docs.rs/integration/index.html)
- App-level system-integration bridge.
- [items](https://docs.rs/items/index.html)
- Per-view `ItemsSource`bridge: populate XAML list controls (`ComboBox`/`ListBox`/`ItemsControl`) from a Bevy app, with typed items.
- [layout](https://docs.rs/layout/index.html)
- Per-view `Margin`writes against named XAML elements: the positioning primitive for floating panels (context menus, popups, tooltips) that must follow gameplay coordinates.
- [list](https://docs.rs/list/index.html)
- **Primitive 2: list = query.**The rows of a XAML list control- *are*Bevy entities: spawn an entity carrying a row-data component and a- `ListedIn`- `ObservableCollection`is reconciled from the query keyed by- `Entity`- **minimal**Add / Remove / Update / Move op sequence (never a- `Clear`/- `Reset`in steady state), so a control’s selection and scroll position survive every edit.
- [markup](https://docs.rs/markup/index.html)
- Custom `MarkupExtension`registration for Bevy.
- [panel](https://docs.rs/panel/index.html)
- **Primitive 1: panel = entity.**A- `UiPanel`- `NoesisView`- *bound components*on that same entity- **are**its- `DataContext`.
- [plain_](https://docs.rs/plain_vm/index.html)- vm
- Per-view plain-struct `ViewModel`bridge: bind a plain Bevy`Component`to a view’s XAML`{Binding field_name}`by field name, two-way.
- [reconcile](https://docs.rs/reconcile/index.html)
- “Diff in parallel, push serially”: the reconcile convention the data-driven bridges (list reconcile, panel/DataContext reconcile) are built on.
- [render](https://docs.rs/render/index.html)
- Render integration: drives each `NoesisView`
- [render_](https://docs.rs/render_device/index.html)- device
- wgpu-backed render device for Noesis. This module pulls in no Bevy types, so you can drive it with a hand-built wgpu instance in tests.
- [resources](https://docs.rs/resources/index.html)
- App-level application-resources bridge. Registers Rust-built resources
(code-built brushes, scalar values) and merged `<ResourceDictionary>`XAML into the process-global application resources, so XAML`{StaticResource Key}`references resolve them without authoring a theme file on disk.
- [routed_](https://docs.rs/routed_events/index.html)- events
- Per-view **generic routed-event**bridge: surface any`RoutedEvent`(mouse, key, focus, drag, manipulation, lifecycle bubbling, …) from named elements of a single`crate::NoesisView`
- [shapes](https://docs.rs/shapes/index.html)
- Per-view shapes bridge: build a Noesis vector `Shape`(`Rectangle`,`Ellipse`, or`Line`) entirely in Rust and assign it as the content of a named XAML container element on a single`NoesisView`
- [styles](https://docs.rs/styles/index.html)
- Per-view code-built `Style`bridge: restyle named XAML elements with a`Noesis::Style`constructed in Rust, no XAML authoring required. The style counterpart of the`crate::dp``crate::brushes`
- [svg](https://docs.rs/svg/index.html)
- Per-view SVG bridge: drive a named XAML element from an SVG *path-data*source string parsed in Rust. The SVG counterpart of the`crate::geometry`
- [text](https://docs.rs/text/index.html)
- Per-view `Text`bridge: write and observe the`Text`of named XAML elements (`TextBox`/`TextBlock`) on a single`crate::NoesisView`
- [theme](https://docs.rs/theme/index.html)
- Opt-in loader for Noesis’s shipped control theme.
- [transforms](https://docs.rs/transforms/index.html)
- Per-view `RenderTransform`writes against named XAML elements: the post-layout scale / skew / rotate / translate that drives UI motion (a button that pops on hover, a panel that slides in, a spinning loader) without touching layout.
- [transforms3d](https://docs.rs/transforms3d/index.html)
- Per-view **3D transform**writes against named XAML elements: the`UIElement.Transform3D`attached behaviour (WinUI/Noesis) that rotates, scales and translates an element in 3D space about a center, with the implicit projection camera supplying perspective. Distinct from the 2D`RenderTransform`bridge (`crate::transforms``RenderTransform`, this one sets`Transform3D`.
- [typography](https://docs.rs/typography/index.html)
- Per-view typography bridge: restyle the `TextElement`font properties (size, family, weight, style, stretch) of named XAML elements on a single`NoesisView`
- [ui](https://docs.rs/ui/index.html)

# cdrip 0.1.5 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cdrip/0.1.5

# CDRip.rs 🎵💽

A fast, accurate CD ripper written in pure Rust. **No GNU dependencies**, no `cdparanoia` system library required.

- **Demo**: Ripping a- **Nirvana In Utero 2CD Deluxe Edition**

## Features

- **Cross-platform**— Windows, Linux, macOS (via direct SCSI commands through- `cd-da-reader`)
- **WAV & FLAC output**— pure-Rust encoders, no native libs needed
- **Retry logic**— configurable per-sector retry count with silence substitution fallback
- **Progress display**— live sector-level progress bars with error/retry counters
- **Rip manifest**— JSON log of every track's result, file size, errors, retries
- **Hidden tracks**— Detect tracks that are hidden inside your CDs
- **Enhanced CD**— Rip CDs with- *extra*media data on it

[!WARNING] For Mac users, some features such as htoa and cd-text are entirely skipped since i have no hardware for it to test, plus Apple's IOKit tight restrictions API.. You're free to contribute if you want to add a platform support.

## Build

```
```
## Install

```
```
## Usage

```
# List detected drives
# Show disc Table of Contents
# Rip entire disc to FLAC (default)
# Rip to WAV
# Rip to MP3
# Rip with ID lookups (musicbrainz, gnudb.org, itunes)
# Scan if a CD has data sections (CD-Extra)
# Generate cue sheets
# Reads a CD-TEXT
# CUE sheet with CD-TEXT populated
# Parallel Encoding
# Detect if a CD has index 00 (also known as HTOA)
# Rip to a specific directory
# Rip only track 3
# Rip with specific device + more retries, keep going on errors
# TUI
# Verbose logging
```
## TUI

**Yet Another CD Ripper** (YACR)

YACR is a TUI application that lets you rip your CDs with interfaces in the terminal! 🐀💿

- **Demo:**Ripping- **Never Enough**by- **Daniel Caesar**

## Output

```
Music/rips/
├── track01.flac
├── track02.flac
├── ...
└── cd-manifest.json
```
`cd-manifest.json` records the rip timestamp, format, per-track sector counts, byte sizes, retry counts, and error counts.

## Architecture

```
src/
├── main.rs         CLI
├── drive.rs        Drive detection & opening (cross-platform)
├── toc.rs          TOC parsing and pretty printer
├── ripper.rs       Sector-level rip loop + retry logic + manifest
├── progress.rs     indicatif progress bars and spinner (weeeeeee)
├── error.rs        thiserror error types
├── parallel.rs     parallel ripping
├── cdtext.rs       CD-TEXT reader
├── cue.rs          Cue Sheets generator
├── htoa.rs         Hidden Track One Audio detection
└── encoder/
    ├── mod.rs      Encoder trait and OutputFormat `enum`
    ├── wav.rs      WAV encoder (hand-rolled RIFF header)
    └── flac.rs     FLAC encoder (flac-codec)
└── id/
    ├── brainz.rs   MusicBrainz id lookup (musicbrainz_rs)
    ├── itunes.rs   iTunes for enrichment (usually cover arts)
    ├── gnudb.rs    GnuDB id lookup
    └── mod.rs      LookupConfig `struct`
```
## Roadmap & TODOs

- TUI frontend (ratatui) with live waveform preview and sector error heatmap
- MusicBrainz disc ID lookup (disc ID derivable from TOC — no extra deps needed)
- CD-TEXT reading (where supported by drive)
- CD-Extra (Enhanced CD) detection and ripping
- MP3 Encoding
- Parallel track ripping
- CUE sheet generation

# What?

Trait objects are serialized by this library like Serde enums. Every impl of the trait (anywhere in the program) looks like one variant of the enum.

All three of Serde's tagged [enum representations](https://serde.rs/enum-representations.html) are supported. The one shown
above is the "internally tagged" style so our two event types would be
represented in JSON as:

Conceptually all you're getting with this crate is that we build for you an enum in which every impl of the trait in your program is automatically registered as an enum variant. The behavior is the same as if you had written the enum yourself and implemented Serialize and Deserialize for the dyn Trait object in terms of the enum.

```
// generated (conceptually)
```
## So many questions

-
*Does it work if the trait impls are spread across different crates?***Yes**Serialization and deserialization both support every single impl of the trait across the dependency graph of the final program binary.
-
*Does it work in non-self-describing data formats like Bincode?***Yes**All three choices of enum representation will round-trip correctly through compact binary formats including Bincode.
-
*Does it support non-struct types?***Yes**The implementations of the trait can be structs, enums, primitives, or anything else supported by Serde. The Serialize and Deserialize impls may be derived or handwritten.
-
*Even in WebAssembly?***Yes**Wasm is supported but with some extra setup described [here](https://docs.rs/inventory/0.3/inventory/index.html#webassembly-and-constructors).
-
*Didn't someone explain to me why this wasn't possible?***Yes**It might have been me.
-
*Then how does it work?*We use the `inventory``ctor``Box<dyn Trait>`deserialization will perform the work of iterating the registry and building a map of tags to deserialization functions. Subsequent deserializations find the right deserialization function in that map. The`erased-serde`

# typetag - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/typetag/0.2.22/target-redirect/typetag/

## Expand description

**Serde serializable and deserializable trait objects.**

This crate provides a macro for painless serialization of `&dyn Trait` trait
objects and serialization + deserialization of `Box<dyn Trait>` trait
objects.

Let’s dive into the example and I’ll explain some more below.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Suppose I have a trait `WebEvent` and I require that every implementation of
the trait be serializable and deserializable so that I can send them to my
ad-serving AI. Here are just the types and trait impls to start with:

```
trait WebEvent {
    fn inspect(&self);
}
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct PageLoad;
impl WebEvent for PageLoad {
    fn inspect(&self) {
        println!("200 milliseconds or bust");
    }
}
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Click {
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
}
impl WebEvent for Click {
    fn inspect(&self) {
        println!("negative space between the ads: x={} y={}", self.x, self.y);
    }
}
```
We’ll need to be able to send an arbitrary web event as JSON to the AI:

```
fn send_event_to_money_factory(event: &dyn WebEvent) -> Result<()> {
    let json = serde_json::to_string(event)?;
    somehow_send_json(json)?;
    Ok(())
}
```
and receive an arbitrary web event as JSON on the server side:

```
fn process_event_from_clickfarm(json: &str) -> Result<()> {
    let event: Box<dyn WebEvent> = serde_json::from_str(json)?;
    overanalyze(event)?;
    Ok(())
}
```
The introduction claimed that this would be painless but I’ll let you be the judge.

First stick an attribute on top of the trait.

```
#[typetag::serde(tag = "type")]
trait WebEvent {
    fn inspect(&self);
}
```
Then stick a similar attribute on all those impl blocks too.

```
#[typetag::serde]
impl WebEvent for PageLoad {
    fn inspect(&self) {
        println!("200 milliseconds or bust");
    }
}
#[typetag::serde]
impl WebEvent for Click {
    fn inspect(&self) {
        println!("negative space between the ads: x={} y={}", self.x, self.y);
    }
}
```
And now it works as described. All in all, three lines were added!

[§](https://docs.rs#what)What?

Trait objects are serialized by this library like Serde enums. Every impl of the trait (anywhere in the program) looks like one variant of the enum.

All three of Serde’s tagged [enum representations](https://serde.rs/enum-representations.html) are supported. The one
shown above is the “internally tagged” style so our two event types would be
represented in JSON as:

```
{"type":"PageLoad"}
{"type":"Click","x":10,"y":10}
```
The choice of enum representation is controlled by the attribute that goes on the trait definition. Let’s check out the “adjacently tagged” style:

```
#[typetag::serde(tag = "type", content = "value")]
trait WebEvent {
    fn inspect(&self);
}
```
```
{"type":"PageLoad","value":null}
{"type":"Click","value":{"x":10,"y":10}}
```
and the “externally tagged” style, which is Serde’s default for enums:

```
#[typetag::serde]
trait WebEvent {
    fn inspect(&self);
}
```
```
{"PageLoad":null}
{"Click":{"x":10,"y":10}}
```
Separately, the value of the tag for a given trait impl may be defined as part of the attribute that goes on the trait impl. By default the tag will be the type name when no name is specified explicitly.

```
#[typetag::serde(name = "mouse_button_down")]
impl WebEvent for Click {
    fn inspect(&self) {
        println!("negative space between the ads: ({}, {})", self.x, self.y);
    }
}
```
`{"type":"mouse_button_down","x":10,"y":10}`Conceptually all you’re getting with this crate is that we build for you an enum in which every impl of the trait in your program is automatically registered as an enum variant. The behavior is the same as if you had written the enum yourself and implemented Serialize and Deserialize for the dyn Trait object in terms of the enum.

```
// generated (conceptually)
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
enum WebEvent {
    PageLoad(PageLoad),
    Click(Click),
    /* ... */
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#so-many-questions)So many questions

-
*Does it work if the trait impls are spread across different crates?***Yes**Serialization and deserialization both support every single impl of the trait across the dependency graph of the final program binary.
-
*Does it work in non-self-describing data formats like Bincode?***Yes**All three choices of enum representation will round-trip correctly through compact binary formats including Bincode.
-
*Does it support non-struct types?***Yes**The implementations of the trait can be structs, enums, primitives, or anything else supported by Serde. The Serialize and Deserialize impls may be derived or handwritten.
-
*Even in WebAssembly?***Yes**Wasm is supported but with some extra setup described [here](https://docs.rs/inventory/0.3/inventory/index.html#webassembly-and-constructors).
-
*Didn’t someone explain to me why this wasn’t possible?***Yes**It might have been me.
-
*Then how does it work?*We use the `inventory``ctor``Box<dyn Trait>`deserialization will perform the work of iterating the registry and building a map of tags to deserialization functions. Subsequent deserializations find the right deserialization function in that map. The`erased-serde`

*Even in WebAssembly?***Yes**Wasm is supported but with some extra setup described [here](https://docs.rs/inventory/0.3/inventory/index.html#webassembly-and-constructors).
-
*Didn’t someone explain to me why this wasn’t possible?***Yes**It might have been me.
-
*Then how does it work?*We use the `inventory``ctor``Box<dyn Trait>`deserialization will perform the work of iterating the registry and building a map of tags to deserialization functions. Subsequent deserializations find the right deserialization function in that map. The`erased-serde`

# typetag/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! [![github]](https://github.com/dtolnay/typetag) [![crates-io]](https://crates.io/crates/typetag) [![docs-rs]](https://docs.rs/typetag)
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! [github]: https://img.shields.io/badge/github-8da0cb?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=555555&logo=github
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! [crates-io]: https://img.shields.io/badge/crates.io-fc8d62?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=555555&logo=rust
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! [docs-rs]: https://img.shields.io/badge/docs.rs-66c2a5?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=555555&logo=docs.rs
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//!
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! <br>
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! **Serde serializable and deserializable trait objects.**
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! This crate provides a macro for painless serialization of `&dyn Trait` trait
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! objects and serialization + deserialization of `Box<dyn Trait>` trait
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! objects.
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//!
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! Let's dive into the example and I'll explain some more below.
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! <br>
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//!
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! # Example
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! Suppose I have a trait `WebEvent` and I require that every implementation of
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! the trait be serializable and deserializable so that I can send them to my
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! ad-serving AI. Here are just the types and trait impls to start with:
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//!
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! ```
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! # use serde::{Serialize, Deserialize};
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! #
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! trait WebEvent {
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!     fn inspect(&self);
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! }
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! struct PageLoad;
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//!
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! impl WebEvent for PageLoad {
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!     fn inspect(&self) {
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//!         println!("200 milliseconds or bust");
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//!     }
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! }
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! struct Click {
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!     x: i32,
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!     y: i32,
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! }
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! impl WebEvent for Click {
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!     fn inspect(&self) {
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//!         println!("negative space between the ads: x={} y={}", self.x, self.y);
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!     }
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! }
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! ```
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//!
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! We'll need to be able to send an arbitrary web event as JSON to the AI:
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//!
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! ```
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! # use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! # use serde_json::Result;
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! #
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! # trait WebEvent {}
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! #
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! # impl<'a> Serialize for dyn WebEvent + 'a {
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! #     fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> std::result::Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! #     where
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! #         S: Serializer,
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! #     {
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! #         unimplemented!()
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! #     }
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! # }
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! #
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! # fn somehow_send_json(json: String) -> Result<()> {
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! #     unimplemented!()
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! # }
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! #
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! fn send_event_to_money_factory(event: &dyn WebEvent) -> Result<()> {
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//!     let json = serde_json::to_string(event)?;
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//!     somehow_send_json(json)?;
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!     Ok(())
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! }
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! ```
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//!
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! and receive an arbitrary web event as JSON on the server side:
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//!
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! ```
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! # use serde::{Deserialize, Deserializer};
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! # use serde_json::Result;
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! #
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! # trait WebEvent {}
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! #
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! # impl<'de> Deserialize<'de> for Box<dyn WebEvent> {
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! #     fn deserialize<D>(deserializer: D) -> std::result::Result<Self, D::Error>
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! #     where
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! #         D: Deserializer<'de>,
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! #     {
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! #         unimplemented!()
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! #     }
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! # }
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! #
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! # fn overanalyze(event: Box<dyn WebEvent>) -> Result<()> {
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! #     unimplemented!()
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! # }
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! #
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! fn process_event_from_clickfarm(json: &str) -> Result<()> {
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//!     let event: Box<dyn WebEvent> = serde_json::from_str(json)?;
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//!     overanalyze(event)?;
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//!     Ok(())
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! }
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! ```
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//!
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! The introduction claimed that this would be painless but I'll let you be the
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! judge.
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//!
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! First stick an attribute on top of the trait.
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//!
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! ```
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! #[typetag::serde(tag = "type")]
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! trait WebEvent {
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//!     fn inspect(&self);
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! }
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! ```
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//!
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//! Then stick a similar attribute on all those impl blocks too.
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//!
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//! ```
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//! # use serde::{Serialize, Deserialize};
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//! #
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//! # #[typetag::serde(tag = "type")]
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! # trait WebEvent {
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//! #     fn inspect(&self);
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! # }
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//! #
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//! # #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//! # struct PageLoad;
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! #
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//! # #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//! # struct Click {
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//! #     x: i32,
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! #     y: i32,
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! # }
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//! #
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! #[typetag::serde]
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//! impl WebEvent for PageLoad {
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//!     fn inspect(&self) {
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//!         println!("200 milliseconds or bust");
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//!     }
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! }
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//!
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! #[typetag::serde]
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//! impl WebEvent for Click {
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//!     fn inspect(&self) {
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//!         println!("negative space between the ads: x={} y={}", self.x, self.y);
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//!     }
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! }
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//! ```
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//!
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//! And now it works as described. All in all, three lines were added!
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//!
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//! <br>
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//!
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//! # What?
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//!
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//! Trait objects are serialized by this library like Serde enums. Every impl of
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//! the trait (anywhere in the program) looks like one variant of the enum.
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//!
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//! All three of Serde's tagged [enum representations] are supported. The one
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//! shown above is the "internally tagged" style so our two event types would be
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//! represented in JSON as:
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//!
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//! [enum representations]: https://serde.rs/enum-representations.html
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//!
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//! ```json
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//! {"type":"PageLoad"}
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//! {"type":"Click","x":10,"y":10}
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//! ```
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//!
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//! The choice of enum representation is controlled by the attribute that goes
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//! on the trait definition. Let's check out the "adjacently tagged" style:
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//!
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//! ```
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//! #[typetag::serde(tag = "type", content = "value")]
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//! trait WebEvent {
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//!     fn inspect(&self);
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//! }
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//! ```
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//!
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//! ```json
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//! {"type":"PageLoad","value":null}
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//! {"type":"Click","value":{"x":10,"y":10}}
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//! ```
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//!
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//! and the "externally tagged" style, which is Serde's default for enums:
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//!
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//! ```
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//! #[typetag::serde]
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//! trait WebEvent {
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//!     fn inspect(&self);
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//! }
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//! ```
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//!
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//! ```json
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//! {"PageLoad":null}
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//! {"Click":{"x":10,"y":10}}
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//! ```
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//!
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//! Separately, the value of the tag for a given trait impl may be defined as
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//! part of the attribute that goes on the trait impl. By default the tag will
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//! be the type name when no name is specified explicitly.
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//!
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//! ```
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//! # use serde::{Serialize, Deserialize};
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//! #
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//! # #[typetag::serde]
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//! # trait WebEvent {
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//! #     fn inspect(&self);
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//! # }
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//! #
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//! # #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//! # struct Click {
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//! #     x: i32,
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//! #     y: i32,
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//! # }
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//! #
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//! #[typetag::serde(name = "mouse_button_down")]
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//! impl WebEvent for Click {
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//!     fn inspect(&self) {
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//!         println!("negative space between the ads: ({}, {})", self.x, self.y);
[227](https://docs.rs#227)//!     }
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//! }
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//! ```
[230](https://docs.rs#230)//!
[231](https://docs.rs#231)//! ```json
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//! {"type":"mouse_button_down","x":10,"y":10}
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//! ```
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//!
[235](https://docs.rs#235)//! Conceptually all you're getting with this crate is that we build for you an
[236](https://docs.rs#236)//! enum in which every impl of the trait in your program is automatically
[237](https://docs.rs#237)//! registered as an enum variant. The behavior is the same as if you had
[238](https://docs.rs#238)//! written the enum yourself and implemented Serialize and Deserialize for the
[239](https://docs.rs#239)//! dyn Trait object in terms of the enum.
[240](https://docs.rs#240)//!
[241](https://docs.rs#241)//! ```
[242](https://docs.rs#242)//! # use serde::{Serialize, Deserialize};
[243](https://docs.rs#243)//! #
[244](https://docs.rs#244)//! # #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
[245](https://docs.rs#245)//! # struct PageLoad;
[246](https://docs.rs#246)//! #
[247](https://docs.rs#247)//! # #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
[248](https://docs.rs#248)//! # struct Click;
[249](https://docs.rs#249)//! #
[250](https://docs.rs#250)//! // generated (conceptually)
[251](https://docs.rs#251)//! #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
[252](https://docs.rs#252)//! enum WebEvent {
[253](https://docs.rs#253)//!     PageLoad(PageLoad),
[254](https://docs.rs#254)//!     Click(Click),
[255](https://docs.rs#255)//!     /* ... */
[256](https://docs.rs#256)//! }
[257](https://docs.rs#257)//! ```
[258](https://docs.rs#258)//!
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//! <br>
[260](https://docs.rs#260)//!
[261](https://docs.rs#261)//! # So many questions
[262](https://docs.rs#262)//!
[263](https://docs.rs#263)//! - *Does it work if the trait impls are spread across different crates?*
[264](https://docs.rs#264)//!   **Yes**
[265](https://docs.rs#265)//!
[266](https://docs.rs#266)//!   Serialization and deserialization both support every single impl of the
[267](https://docs.rs#267)//!   trait across the dependency graph of the final program binary.
[268](https://docs.rs#268)//!
[269](https://docs.rs#269)//! - *Does it work in non-self-describing data formats like Bincode?* **Yes**
[270](https://docs.rs#270)//!
[271](https://docs.rs#271)//!   All three choices of enum representation will round-trip correctly through
[272](https://docs.rs#272)//!   compact binary formats including Bincode.
[273](https://docs.rs#273)//!
[274](https://docs.rs#274)//! - *Does it support non-struct types?* **Yes**
[275](https://docs.rs#275)//!
[276](https://docs.rs#276)//!   The implementations of the trait can be structs, enums, primitives, or
[277](https://docs.rs#277)//!   anything else supported by Serde. The Serialize and Deserialize impls may
[278](https://docs.rs#278)//!   be derived or handwritten.
[279](https://docs.rs#279)//!
[280](https://docs.rs#280)//! - *Even in WebAssembly?* **Yes**
[281](https://docs.rs#281)//!
[282](https://docs.rs#282)//!   Wasm is supported but with some extra setup described [here][wasm].
[283](https://docs.rs#283)//!
[284](https://docs.rs#284)//!   [wasm]: https://docs.rs/inventory/0.3/inventory/index.html#webassembly-and-constructors
[285](https://docs.rs#285)//!
[286](https://docs.rs#286)//! - *Didn't someone explain to me why this wasn't possible?* **Yes**
[287](https://docs.rs#287)//!
[288](https://docs.rs#288)//!   It might have been me.
[289](https://docs.rs#289)//!
[290](https://docs.rs#290)//! - *Then how does it work?*
[291](https://docs.rs#291)//!
[292](https://docs.rs#292)//!   We use the [`inventory`] crate to produce a registry of impls of your
[293](https://docs.rs#293)//!   trait, which is built on the [`ctor`] crate to hook up initialization
[294](https://docs.rs#294)//!   functions that insert into the registry. The first `Box<dyn Trait>`
[295](https://docs.rs#295)//!   deserialization will perform the work of iterating the registry and
[296](https://docs.rs#296)//!   building a map of tags to deserialization functions. Subsequent
[297](https://docs.rs#297)//!   deserializations find the right deserialization function in that map. The
[298](https://docs.rs#298)//!   [`erased-serde`] crate is also involved, to do this all in a way that does
[299](https://docs.rs#299)//!   not break object safety.
[300](https://docs.rs#300)//!
[301](https://docs.rs#301)//! [`inventory`]: https://github.com/dtolnay/inventory
[302](https://docs.rs#302)//! [`ctor`]: https://github.com/mmastrac/rust-ctor
[303](https://docs.rs#303)//! [`erased-serde`]: https://github.com/dtolnay/erased-serde
[304](https://docs.rs#304)
[305](https://docs.rs#305)#![no_std]
[306](https://docs.rs#306)#![doc(html_root_url = "https://docs.rs/typetag/0.2.22")]
[307](https://docs.rs#307)#![allow(
[308](https://docs.rs#308)    clippy::elidable_lifetime_names,
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    clippy::missing_errors_doc,

[311](https://docs.rs#311)    clippy::needless_lifetimes,
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    clippy::uninlined_format_args,
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    clippy::unnested_or_patterns
[314](https://docs.rs#314))]
[315](https://docs.rs#315)#![allow(unknown_lints, mismatched_lifetime_syntaxes)]

# serde in typetag - Rust
